lesson.title: Picture First: Drawing the Related Rates Diagram
lesson.summary: A single, carefully labeled diagram, drawn at one frozen instant with variables instead of numbers, turns a wordy related rates story into a geometry problem you already know how to solve.
lesson.body:
Related rates word problems describe a scene that is actually changing over time, a ladder sliding, a balloon expanding, a shadow lengthening, but at any one frozen instant, that changing scene is just an ordinary static picture: a right triangle, a circle, a cone. The purpose of the diagram is to capture that static picture clearly enough that you can read a geometric equation straight off of it, which is exactly what step three of the related rates setup method needs.

A good related rates diagram follows a few simple rules. Draw the scene as it looks at a generic moment, not at the very start and not at the final instant described in the problem, so the labeled quantities are still free to represent any value they might take. Label every quantity that changes with a letter, x, y, r, h, and label every quantity that stays fixed for the whole problem with its actual number, since that is the only kind of quantity allowed to appear as a number before you differentiate. It also helps to mark the rate you are given, often with a small arrow, and to mark the rate you are asked to find with a question mark, so the goal of the problem is visible at a glance.

Here is a small example that shows a diagram leading directly to an equation. A rectangle has width x and height y, with a diagonal z connecting opposite corners, forming a right triangle with legs x and y and hypotenuse z. Suppose that, at some instant, x = 4 centimeters and y = 3 centimeters, with the width growing at dx/dt = 1 centimeter per second and the height growing at dy/dt = 2 centimeters per second. How fast is the diagonal growing at that instant? The diagram itself, a right triangle with legs x and y and hypotenuse z, hands you the equation immediately: z^2 = x^2 + y^2, the Pythagorean theorem. At this instant, z^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 = 16 + 9 = 25, so z = 5. Differentiating with respect to t: 2z (dz/dt) = 2x (dx/dt) + 2y (dy/dt), and dividing by 2 gives z (dz/dt) = x (dx/dt) + y (dy/dt). Substituting: 5 (dz/dt) = 4(1) + 3(2) = 4 + 6 = 10, so dz/dt = 2 centimeters per second.

Every classic related rates problem that follows, a ladder against a wall, an inflating balloon, a shadow cast by a streetlight, a draining conical tank, two cars pulling apart from an intersection, begins with exactly this kind of picture. The equation you write down for each one, the Pythagorean theorem, a volume formula, a similar triangles ratio, comes directly from reading the diagram correctly, which is why getting comfortable with this labeling habit now pays off across all five of the problems ahead.
